The Almoravid Dynasty. From 1056 to 1147 of the common era, this was a Berber military movement that emerged from the Sahara Desert, conquered the western Maghreb and Islamic Spain, and restored puritanical Islamic orthodoxy to a fragmented region. Though their rule was geographically vast and militarily powerful, the Almoravids were eventually overthrown by a more zealous reformist movement—the Almohads—whom they had inadvertently inspired.

The Almoravids were founded by Abdallah ibn Yasin, a puritanical Islamic reformer, as a desert monastic movement. The name itself, al-murabitun, means those bound by religious duty. Under his leadership they united fractious Saharan Berber tribes under strict Islamic law. Then in the 1070s, under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, they conquered the Maghreb and established a capital at Marrakesh in 1071. That city became one of the Islamic world's most magnificent centers. They intervened in Islamic Spain at the invitation of embattled taifa, or petty, kings, halting the Christian Reconquista and winning the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086. But rather than protecting their allies, they annexed Spanish territories instead. The Almoravids enforced a literalist, fundamentalist interpretation of Islam that suppressed philosophical inquiry and theological innovation, earning them a reputation as rigid and intolerant. They controlled the lucrative trans-Saharan gold trade from West Africa, accumulating wealth that funded monumental architecture in Marrakesh and Cordoba. Yet by 1147 they succumbed to the Almohad movement, another Berber reformist dynasty that denounced them as insufficiently rigorous and captured their territories.

The Almohads succeeded and supplanted them. They influenced Islamic Spain, Al-Andalus, where they briefly intervened. The Umayyad Caliphate had been the earlier Islamic Spanish power they sought to restore. And the fragmented Christian and Muslim kingdoms of medieval Spain, the taifas, were caught in their wake.
